Frontiers in Marine Science

Ibrahim A, Alkarbi N, Alsaadi M, Almazrouei A, Alshamsi S and Hamouda MA (2026). Satellite-based machine learning models for chlorophyll-a and TSS retrieval in Abu Dhabi's coastal waters. Frontiers in Marine Science 13:1787597. doi: 10.3389/fmars.2026.1787597

Satellite Eyes on the Coast AI-Driven Water Quality Monitoring for Abu Dhabi's Coastal Waters

Sentinel-2 images and machine learning, trained on routine field samples from 22 monitoring sites, retrieve chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) and total suspended solids (TSS) along the Abu Dhabi coast. A model built for typical conditions cut the average Chl-a error from 8.21 to 1.62 μg/L.

QuestionCan free satellite images track algae and sediment in optically complex Gulf waters?
ApproachMatchups in Google Earth Engine, two feature strategies, four tuned ML algorithms.
ResultChl-a: Test R² 0.70, RMSE 1.62 μg/L. TSS: Test R² 0.61. Coast-wide maps at 20 m.

1. Rationale: the need

Protecting the coastal water behind the UAE's water supply

The UAE depends mainly on groundwater and desalinated water, so the quality of its coastal water is tied to both environmental protection and public safety. Detecting and controlling pollution requires tracking water quality across space and time, yet remote sensing algorithms tailored to UAE coastal waters are still lacking.

  • Chl-a is the key indicator of eutrophication and algal blooms; high TSS and turbidity signal sediment, organic matter and habitat degradation.
  • High temperatures, a dry climate, urban runoff and desalination discharge make Gulf water quality hard to monitor.
  • Harmful algal bloom events push Chl-a far above typical levels: up to 104.51 μg/L against a mean of 4.58 μg/L.
  • Field sampling and laboratory analysis are time-consuming and labour-intensive, with limited coverage in space and time.
  • Sentinel-2 imagery is free, with 10 to 60 m pixels and a 5-day revisit, giving coverage that field programmes cannot reach.

2. Rationale: the problem

Global ocean-colour algorithms misread Gulf water

The Arabian Gulf is a "Case II" environment: sediment and dissolved organic matter change the water's colour independently of algae. Standard algorithms were built for open ocean, and global products are too coarse to see the shoreline where problems start.

Problem statement

Abu Dhabi's coastal water is monitored at a few dozen points by boat, while the satellite tools built for open ocean overestimate chlorophyll here and cannot resolve the shallow nearshore water where blooms and sediment plumes appear. Without a regionally trained, high-resolution retrieval, agencies cannot see water quality across the whole coast between field visits.

3. Research gaps and questions

Four gaps, one objective, three research questions

The gaps concern which tools work in arid, optically complex coastal water and how to treat bloom events.

Main objective

To develop machine learning models that retrieve Chl-a and TSS from Sentinel-2 surface reflectance in Abu Dhabi's coastal waters, tuned to the region's conditions and checked against ground-truth measurements.

4. What has been done

Sentinel-2 works on coasts elsewhere; the Gulf has relied on coarse data

Studies from Vietnam to Morocco report moderate to high accuracy with Sentinel-2 and machine learning. In the Gulf, the closest work used 1 km MODIS time series.

7. Results

A specialized model cut the Chl-a error by 80%

XGB on PCA of six bands was the best Chl-a model. Trained on ambient conditions it reached Test R² 0.70 with an average error of 1.62 μg/L. For TSS, PCA with Random Forest reached Test R² 0.61 from only 77 points.

9. The big picture

From one sampling station to SDG 6 and SDG 14

The 2026 UN Water Conference meets in Abu Dhabi to accelerate progress on SDG 6, clean water and sanitation for all. This work gives a low-cost way to watch water quality across a whole coastline, using free satellite data and the monitoring an agency already runs. The same signal tracks coastal eutrophication under SDG 14, life below water.

Ground truth

10. For discussion

From validated models to coast-wide monitoring

XGB on PCA of six bands retrieves Chl-a with Test R² 0.70 and an average error of 1.62 μg/L under ambient conditions, and Random Forest on PCA retrieves TSS with Test R² 0.61. Turning these models into routine monitoring raises three questions for agencies and researchers: how satellite maps fit alongside field sampling, how to capture blooms and plumes, and how far the workflow transfers to other arid coasts.

  1. How could satellite maps sit alongside routine boat sampling in agency programmes?Satellites complement field sampling rather than replace it.
  2. How can more samples be collected during blooms and turbidity plumes?Both models underestimate extremes for lack of high values.
  3. Could the same workflow be calibrated for other Gulf and arid coasts?Regional calibration with local field data is what made it work.

Beyond ambient conditions

Open extension

Possible extension

Localized, nutrient-driven blooms near coastal outlets form a separate biogeochemical regime. A dedicated bloom model, trained on more high-concentration samples, would complete the pair: the ambient model for routine monitoring and a bloom model to detect and size events.
